title: Bubble would be trouble as AI fears emerge
full_text:
ENERGY NATION The Albanese government’s Digital Economy Minister Andrew Charlton has warned of an AI investment bubble and has played down the Prime Minister’s decision to retreat from a call for states to have large data centres powered by renewable energy only.
Dr Charlton warned that not allowing flexibility in how data centre investors add energy to the grid would risk the delivery of cheaper electricity and would become an election issue.
“If we get these ingredients right, data centres become what the evidence say they can be. They become anchor tenants for a new generation. If we get them wrong and we import America’s price shock, we will deserve the political consequences,” he told The Australian’s Energy Nation forum in Sydney on Wednesday.
“In the (US) midterms, the data centre issue is becoming a top-tier political issue in a lot of races, and justifiably so. Those negative consequences have had real impacts. We want to learn from that experience.” Queensland Premier David Crisafulli, who also attended Energy Nation, said he thought Anthony Albanese showed “maturity” by reversing a recent decision to mandate states to power large AI data centres with only renewable energy, warning a $31bn deal with AI juggernaut Anthropic would have been killed by the measure.
After a meeting of national cabinet, the Prime Minister backed down on measures to override states on the sources of energy generation for data centres, allowing Queensland to tap into its gas reserves and coal-fired power to power the AI buildout.
Noting in tongue and cheek that Dr Charlton had not mentioned coal and gas – and as a result he would not mention Energy Minister Chris Bowen – Mr Crisafulli said while the backdown was a win for Queensland, he would still require data centre developers to contribute to new energy generation. “There was a decision taken, and I think it showed maturity from the Prime Minister,” Mr Crisafulli said.
Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki suggested Mr Albanese and Mr Bowen were at odds with each other.
“The Premier reflected on it briefly about the pragmatic streak that was shown by the Prime Minister, but Chris Bowen doesn’t share the Queensland approach to data centres,” Mr Janetzki said.
Dr Charlton brushed over the backdown.
“Government has been very clear on this question in relation to our interaction with the states,” Dr Charlton said.
“That is, the commonwealth is setting these standards, these Australian AI standards that the Prime Minister announced a month or two ago in his AI speech in Sydney. Those standards will be a floor, not a ceiling.
“And to the extent that states want to introduce their own rules that are consistent with that floor, and account for local variation in this in their states, that is spelled out in the discussion paper as being consistent.” SGH chief executive Ryan Stokes weighed into the debate, saying he thought the government’s calls for data centres to be solely powered by renewable energy “defies a fundamental logic” and that AI infrastructure required 24/7 power.
Pointing to the US buildout of data centres, Mr Stokes claimed there was a distinct lack of discussion of the role of gas in Australia’s own approach to the investment boom.
“The idea that that a data centre can be solely powered by renewables, I think, defies a fundamental logic, like what happens at night when these things need to run,” Mr Stockes told The Australian’s Energy Nation forum.
“There is no real talk about the role that gas has.
“And you look at what’s happening in the US and the building of data centres next to gas pipelines for that very clear reason. They need that that reliable, affordable energy source to power these data centres 24/7.” This week Reserve Bank governor Michelle Bullock said she was uncertain as to whether the trillion of dollars in AI investment was a bubble.
“It might not be a bubble, but it might be. And if it unwinds in a disorderly manner, then that could have implications for the financial system and also for the real economies,” Ms Bullock told a CEDA event.
Amid an estimated $180bn in AI investment expected in Australia from companies such as Nvidia, Anthropic, OpenAI, Amazon, Google and Microsoft, Dr Charlton on Wednesday said the question was more about what part of the AI boom was more susceptible to bubble conditions.
“The question that the markets are asking in relation to ‘is this a bubble’ is not is the demand there, but will the revenue be there?” he said.
“Will there be enough revenue to pay back the extraordinary investment costs of this boom? In order to pay back the capital that’s been invested in that boom, the data centres will need $2 trillion of revenue.
“They are currently on track for around half of that. Now, that trajectory could change. But to the extent that people talk about this being a bubble, that’s the concern. “Will the revenue be there? That’s the question.”
